title: Making Special Weapons Unique (with basic editor function)

posts.author: jonthefox
posts.body:
I'd like ideas or some new things to think about when it comes to making different weapons feel distinctive.  Often as you discover unique weapons as you go through a game, it just comes with higher stats, which feels a bit boring.
The thing is, it is easy to think of cool ideas *IN THEORY* - but often they would require plugins or a bunch of programming knowledge.  I'm looking for things that can be done with the basic editor, and just require some outside the box thinking.
Also:  I don't really want to give weapons their own unique damage formula, since I'd like weapon attributes to still be present when you use various skills (which THEMSELVES have their own unique damage formulas).
Looking forward to hearing people's ideas and opinions!

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
You put this in Game Mechanics Design, which is editor-agnostic, but the fact of the matter is your possibilities greatly depend on the editor you're using. Especially since you say you want to use no plugins, for some reason.
MZ has much more options than any other engine, with the addition of the Attack Skill trait - you can make any weapon use its own skill for attack, so they can do anything you can configure in a skill in the database.
But, then, if you're saying you only want to discuss things that are properties of the weapon that apply to other skills that you use...and you don't want to use plugins...you're pretty darned limited. Open up the Traits window and see what there is
Or you can attach common events to your skills which check for which weapon the user is wielding and add some kind of other effects after the skill has gone off.

posts.author: NamEtag
posts.body:
For a weapon to modify physical skills, it needs to have an attribute that the skill actively checks for use. Normally that's the ATK stat, but you don't want to change the damage formula.
So it's going to be a mechanic that the skill triggers, or a state it applies.....without plugins....
To a certain degree, you're better off with the weapon having a passive or skill that activates whenever you use a physical skill.

posts.author: jerrylikesgreen
posts.body:
My approach would be to focus less on a weapon's direct impact in battle, like attacking or influencing stats, and more on how it shapes the game's experience. This can be achieved using a mix of variables, events, and states, depending on the level of complexity you're aiming for.
Visuals and audio are powerful tools to enhance the epicness of a moment. For instance, when a character equips a weapon, you could trigger a transformation by changing their state to "Empowered," which then sets off a series of events: changing the player sprite, adding sound effects, or even altering the background music to something more intense. Imagine a Super Saiyan transformation from Dragon Ball Z—simple changes like these can make the moment feel monumental. All of which can be done with no plugins or scripting involved.
The possibilities are endless; that was just a quick idea to illustrate the concept.
If you'd like more assistance or a brainstorming partner to bounce ideas off of, let me know. Sometimes, having someone to collaborate with can really get the creative juices flowing.

My intention wasn't for the transformation to occur immediately upon equipping the item. Instead, I envisioned it as a state change that occurs after equipping, where the sprite updates to reflect this new state. To enhance the experience, we could also incorporate audio cues, like bell chimes, to highlight the transition into this new state. I apologize for any confusion on that point.
Essentially, the flow would be: you open the item or equipment screen, equip the weapon, and your character's state changes as a result. When you return to the game, your character appears transformed, and the game's audio changes to reflect this transformation. I apologize if I wasn't clear before—I sometimes struggle to express my ideas in words.
Regarding the idea of having a parallel process constantly checking the player's status, I agree that it would be inefficient. That approach wasn't my proposed solution. What I intended to suggest is that the game engine offers numerous ways to integrate your weapons outside of battle, which could help make them feel more unique and special.
If we decide to explore this transformation concept further, we should consider a few key factors: the specific mechanics of how the transformation will occur, the reasoning behind it, how it fits within the game's context, and what existing mechanics can be utilized to support this transformation.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I guess I'm not sure what you're asking for here.  What do you consider "distinctive"?  I have stuff that is "distinctive" for my game, and maybe a couple items "distinctive" for other games.
"Preserve TP" items are an insane rarity within my game, so any weapon that has that on it, is very rare, powerful, and quite distinctive to my game.
But, I also have "Walken Stick", which is a staff that is above average in Magic Defense and MP gained.  It has a description of "I got a fever!" and when used it makes a cowbell sound.  If ya get the joke, ya get the joke.
Before I can suggest anything, I'm going to need specifically what you're looking for, since what you're asking is "subjective" and can be dependent on the setting/typical abilities within the game itself.
As an example, in a low magic game where no items come with elemental effects, a Fire Sword would be insanely memorable and rare.

posts.author: Robro33
posts.body:
you could play around with your elements to make sub elements for weapons.
default mv/z behavior towards multiple attack elements on battler is to use the most effective one iirc. so weapons can have physical as an attack element and a secondary one like slash/bash/pierce that you can use to make situations where they specifically do more damage.
you could do something like "make hammers better against stone enemies" by giving each hammer phys+bash as attack elements, and then make the stone enemies resistant to phys and weak to bash. you end up with hammers ignoring the phys resistance and exploiting the bash weakness, while others would just hit the phys resistance. the caveat is that you'd have to keep track of all of these for all enemies. if you forget to make a stone enemy strong against slash while its strong to phys, phys only weapons deal reduced damage while swords with slashing will just do normal damage

It's always a bit tricky with turn based games, because you can't mix it up with stuff like movesets or anything.
What you can do, is give weapons unique skills. I've been playing the FF7 remake, and every weapon has a unique skill. Using that skill a bunch with permanently learn it.
Obviously you don't have to do that exact thing, but it's a start.
Other than that, weapons that inflict states are always fun, especially if you can switch weapons mid battle.
Changing animations and sound effects will also help it feel more unique.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Eh, I work strictly within MV, and I'm not even sure anything I do would be "distinctive enough".
I'm particularly proud of my own "niche" weapons/equipment, but I don't think that applies to this topic since they're "generalized categories".
I mean, just as some examples:
Dagger -
Weak weapon, but always comes with status effects as part of its draw.  Since status effects are powerful in my game, then it might not necessarily be that you want more attack power, but a better chance to inflict Poison or Paralyze on hit instead.
Katar
- As weak as the Dagger (just in a different way), but typically comes with a chance for Counter Attack and a high chance to land a critical hit.
Wand -
Very low damage, but always inflicts "Weakness to X" on hit.  It can do this for 1 element or multiple elements.  I have a lot of elements in my game, so picking a wand is less about "How much overall damage" the weapon itself does, and more what you want to "follow up" or "support other party members" with.  It also gives mages a good reason to just hit the "Attack" button in combat when out of MP.
Orb
- Has no attack damage what-so-ever.  Attacking with it changes the element of your "Attack" command to "Magic" as well as any other element attached to the Orb.  Essentially, it's the mages' version of an elemental sword, except it can usually hit at least two other elements besides "Magic".
Book
- This is actually classified as a "Shield" within my game, but it does something decently unique in that is provides 100% immunity to specific elements.  This can be a whole Category (like Strength, Magic, or Speed) or a specific Element (like Water).
Battle Axe
- This is "the most damaging class of weapons" in the entire game, but their accuracy starts at 75% and can go down from there as you equip more and more powerful ones.
---
Basically, I have "categories" and then "tiers" of equipment so that the stat spread is pretty much evened out.  Players are meant to "fire and forget" their weapons in most cases and only pick the "kind of weapon" they want each character to use most of the time, and then decide what works best within that category for their character builds.  So, there are "side grades" and "weird niches" within those tiers and categories, but it's all highly situational.
Heck, I even have a Claymore that is "Blunt" element and also has its defense/attack stats switched around so that it can basically be used for tanking (instead of the 16 attack and 8 defense it would normally confer, it gives 4 attack and 20 defense).  Without a player building their characters for using that kind of niche weapon, it would basically just be a very "limited use case" type of thing.

...so this is one of the things I do XD New actions can absolutely be a reason to make new equipment awesome, especially if that's the main reason for that equip slot (such as determining what your basic attack is). For something even more widespread, I had one game where everyone learned spells but only one character naturally had the Magic skill type, so any piece of equipment that gave Magic added a slew of additional options (especially when it's a staff that removes physical skills!).
But in the general sense, I largely stopped having weapons that are just "Attack go up". Sometimes it's as simple as a different number also going up, sometimes it's adding a trait, sometimes it's new immunities, and sometimes it fully changes what a character can do.

Unfortunately, that breaks how my game plays.  It's about combat mastery and managing resources.  If the player could just whack enemies before a boss fight to regen all their MP, then it defeats the point of having to manage the resource through the whole dungeon.
My players are meant to be buying MP Restoring Consumables and using them.  Combat mastery is when they don't need to use much MP, or many consumables, to fight their way to the boss.
